extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in U.S. patent law and case law (law students, IP practitioners, litigators, interested public)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the legal standards and criteria used by U.S. courts (Federal Circuit and Supreme Court) to determine when method-patent infringement can be attributed across multiple actors (divided infringement), including when indirect/induced liability applies. Focuses on attribution doctrines like control/direction, agency/contract, conditioning/benefit, and joint-enterprise rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct infringement requires single actor or attributable steps
rubrics_metrics.description: To find direct infringement a single party must perform every step of a claimed method or else must exercise 'control or direction' over the entire process so that 'every step is attributable to the controlling party.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the baseline traditional rule cited by the Federal Circuit: a method claim is directly infringed only when one actor performs all steps or the other actors' performances are attributable to that actor. Examples: where defendant physically performs all steps, or where other actors are their agents or are under their control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribution via agency relationship or contractual obligation (Muniauction rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant that does not itself perform all of a patent's steps can be liable for direct infringement only when there is an agency relationship between the parties who perform the other method steps or when one party is contractually obligated to the other to perform the steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit panel decisions (e.g., Muniauction) held that agency or contractual obligations suffice to attribute others' acts to the defendant. This was applied to deny liability where such relationships were absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induced infringement (§271(b)) cannot occur without direct infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that induced patent infringement cannot occur without direct infringement — i.e., there must be an act of direct infringement by someone before inducement liability can attach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: permitting inducement without direct infringement would deprive §271(b) of ascertainable standards and create parallel bodies of law. Practical effect: courts must determine whether direct infringement occurred (including attribution issues) before finding inducement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded vicarious liability: conditioning participation/benefit and establishing manner/timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Liability under §271(a) can be found when an alleged infringer 'conditions participation in an activity or receipt of a benefit upon performance of a step or steps of a patented method and establishes the manner or timing of that performance.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the Federal Circuit's en banc addition (Akamai 2015) to the attribution doctrines; it parallels copyright vicarious liability. Facts supporting this include contractual terms or business practices that make use of a service contingent on customers performing claim steps and that dictate how/when they do so (e.g., Limelight's form contract requiring customer tagging and establishing timing/manner).

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint enterprise vicarious liability — four Restatement elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple actors form a joint enterprise, each may be charged with the acts of the others as if each were a single actor. Proof requires the four elements from Restatement (Second) of Torts §491 cmt. b: (1) an agreement, express or implied, among the members of the group; (2) a common purpose to be carried out by the group; (3) a community of pecuniary interest in that purpose, among the members; and (4) an equal right to a voice in the direction of the enterprise, which gives an equal right of control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the four elements are met, acts by any member within the scope of the enterprise can be attributed vicariously to all. Whether a joint enterprise exists is a question of fact for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed-or-controlled fact question — substantial-evidence review on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a single actor directed or controlled the acts of one or more third parties is a question of fact, reviewable on appeal for substantial evidence, when tried to a jury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the 'direct/control' attribution and the 'joint enterprise' attribution raise fact questions appropriate for jury resolution; appellate courts assess adequacy of evidence under the substantial-evidence standard rather than de novo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere instruction or assistance is insufficient absent conditioning or control
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing instructions or technical assistance to others does not automatically make a defendant liable for direct infringement; the defendant must have conditioned participation/benefit or exercised control such that steps are attributable to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Medgraph v. Medtronic) hold that telling users how to perform steps is not enough if the defendant neither requires performance nor conditions use/benefit on performance, nor establishes manner/timing. Courts look to whether the accused infringer denies benefits or otherwise coerces compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product labeling/instructions can create attribution when they condition benefit and specify manner/timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory labeling or instructions that (a) instruct a party how to perform steps and (b) make receipt of the claimed benefit contingent on performing those steps can satisfy the 'conditioning participation/benefit' and 'establishing manner or timing' tests, thereby attributing the steps to the party who issues the instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: in Lilly v. Teva, FDA-required labeling instructed physicians/patients to follow a regimen (start folic acid at specified dosage/timing) and stated that failure to do so would deprive the patient of the benefit; the district court found these facts analogous to Akamai and sufficient to attribute patient steps to physicians and to sustain induced-infringement claims against generic manufacturers who provided the instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application threshold: evidence must show performance of the missing steps by the relevant actors
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed under the expanded attribution theories, a patentee must present evidence that the missing claim steps were actually performed by the other actors (and that the defendant's conduct made those performances attributable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Medgraph, the patentee failed because it could not show that the missing steps were actually performed or that the defendant conditioned use/benefit on them. Courts require both proof of performance and proof of attribution criteria (control/conditioning/joint enterprise).
